description: In Chiricahua and Mescalero Apache tradition, the Sun is the great creator deity who brought light and order to the world. Their creation story begins with a great flood that destroyed a malevolent world, and the creator, closely linked to the Sun, shaped the world, the gods, and all living things through his power.
source: Morris Opler, 'An Apache Life-Way'; Chiricahua and Mescalero Apache oral tradition; Southwestern ethnographic records
research_notes: Attested. The Chiricahua/Mescalero creation account opens with a great flood that destroyed a malevolent world, after which the creator emerged; the input's 'Sun' framing reflects the Apache association of the supreme being (Ussen/the creator) with the sun. Personification of the Sun is strongest in Chiricahua and Mescalero ceremonialism, though the creator is often described in more impersonal terms.

description: The Sacred Birds of Summerland are the origin of the small birds in Zuni tradition. A Zuni man found a magical bundle of feathers left by the spirits, and when he walked into a field of flowers the bundle burst open, releasing small wings that became jaybirds, sparrows, finches and all the bright little birds that herald the return of summer.
source: Zuni oral tradition; in-repo story 'How the Summer Birds Came'
research_notes: Attested. The origin-of-small-birds tale is recorded as the Zuni story 'How the Summer Birds Came' and matches the input's summary: a feather bundle left by spirits unfolds in a flower field and releases the first small songbirds. 'Summerland' is an English gloss; the Zuni concept ties these birds to the return of the summer season.

description: The Suuke are cave-dwelling monsters of Zuni tradition, lesser demonic beings who live in the cliffs and caves around Zuni lands. They carry off children in their baskets, and are counted among the dangerous supernatural creatures associated with Atahsaia, the terrible man-eating ogre of Zuni legend.
source: native-languages.org Zuni Legends (Suuke, Atahsaia); Zuni oral tradition
research_notes: Attested. Native-languages.org records the Suuke as Zuni monsters 'said to live in caves and carry off children in their baskets,' confirming the input. Their association with Atahsaia (A'tahsaia), the cannibal ogre, matches the recorded Zuni monster tradition, though the Suuke themselves are lesser beings described as cave-dwelling child-snatchers.

description: Sky Woman (Atsi'tsaká:ion, 'Mature Flower') is the primordial mother of Haudenosaunee (Iroquois) creation. She fell from the Sky World through a hole left by an uprooted tree, landed on the back of the Great Turtle, and with a handful of mud brought up by the water animals the earth was created; her line bore the twins who shaped the world.
source: native-languages.org Iroquois Legends; sacred-texts.com; Wikipedia 'Iroquois mythology'
research_notes: Attested and expert-sourced. Atsi'tsaká:ion means 'Mature Flower' (often rendered Ataensic in older transcriptions), and the descent, landing on Turtle's back, and earth-from-mud motif match the Haudenosaunee account. The input's 'she gave birth to the twins' is a slight compression: in the classic version her daughter is the mother of the twins, but the aliases and core story are sound.

description: Selu, the Corn Mother, is the First Woman of Cherokee tradition and wife of Kanati the Great Hunter. By rubbing her body she produced corn and beans from her own flesh, and when her sons discovered her secret she accepted her death, instructing that her body be dragged across the field so that corn would grow where she fell.
source: James Mooney, 'Myths of the Cherokee' (1900); native-languages.org Cherokee Legends
research_notes: Attested; expert source (Mooney 1900). Selu (Cherokee for 'corn') is the Corn Mother who rubbed her body to make corn and beans and, after her secret was discovered, instructed that her body be dragged so corn would grow from it. The input's 'first woman' claim matches Cherokee tradition, where Selu and Kanati are the first family.

description: Spearfinger, Nûñ'yunu'ï or U'tlun'ta, is a cannibal witch of Cherokee tradition who roamed the mountains of eastern Tennessee and western North Carolina. An old woman armored in stone with a long, sharp forefinger, she cut out the livers of careless travelers and children; only the vulnerable spot on her palm allowed her to be slain.
source: James Mooney, 'Myths of the Cherokee' (1900), tale of U'tlun'ta; native-languages.org Cherokee Legends
research_notes: Attested; expert source (Mooney). Nûñ'yunu'ï ('Stone-Dress') / U'tlun'ta matches the input: a stone-clad old woman with a spear-like forefinger who ate livers, vulnerable only on a point of her palm. The record's weakness (arrows piercing the palm) is accurate to the legend, and the geographic setting (eastern Tennessee / western NC mountains) is confirmed.

description: The Stikini are dreaded owl-witches of Seminole folklore. By day they look like ordinary people, but at night they vomit up their souls and internal organs and become undead owl-monsters with bloodshot eyes that feed on human hearts. In some communities, saying the name aloud is itself thought to risk transformation.
source: native-languages.org Seminole Legends (Stikini)
research_notes: Attested. Native-languages.org documents the Stikini as Seminole owl-witches who appear human by day and become undead owl-monsters by night, vomiting up their souls and organs to hunt human hearts; some communities avoid saying the name. The input's nightly owl-transformation is accurate, and the heart-eating detail is confirmed.

description: Sint-Holo is the horned serpent of Chickasaw and Choctaw tradition, a great water serpent who dwells in rivers, lakes and springs. Dangerous to those who disrespect it, it drags careless people to watery deaths, yet it also appears as a spirit guide during fasting, bestowing power and gifts on the worthy; it is the avowed enemy of the Thunder spirits.
source: native-languages.org Chickasaw Legends (Sint-Holo / Sintholo)
research_notes: Attested. Native-languages.org records Sint-Holo (Sintholo) as a horned water serpent shared by Chickasaw and Choctaw tradition. Confirmed traits: dwells in deep waters, dangerous and drags people to watery death, but a powerful spirit guide during fasting that grants gifts, and an enemy of the Thunder spirits. The input's purely Chickasaw framing is slightly narrow; the figure is shared with the Choctaw.

description: Sisiutl is a supernatural sea serpent of the Kwakwaka'wakw, usually shown as a double-headed snake with two horned serpent heads flanking a central human face, its body marked with crescents. Its glance can turn a person to stone, yet it also grants protective power, and can transform into an invincible war canoe or a warrior's magic belt.
source: Franz Boas, 'Kwakiutl Tales' (1910); Wikipedia 'Kwakwaka'wakw mythology' (Sisiutl)
research_notes: Attested; expert source (Boas 1910). The Sisiutl is a genuine Kwakwaka'wakw being: double-headed serpent with a central humanoid face, crescent markings, a petrifying glance, and transformations into a war canoe or magic belt (Wikipedia; Boas). The common 'three-headed' description actually refers to the two serpent heads plus the central human face. Country should be Canada (Kwakwaka'wakw are British Columbia), though the tribe field is correct.

description: Skimina is the granddaughter of the Nuxalk (Bella Coola) creator Alhkw'ntam, who lives in the upper world. In the story of how Raven gave light to the world, she unknowingly holds the transforming Raven as he changes into a baby, and her care of the crying child lets him reach the box where the sun was hidden.
source: Nuxalk Nation official site (Ximkila Totem Pole narrative); Franz Boas, 'The Mythology of the Bella Coola Indians' (1898)
research_notes: Attested; confirmed directly by the Nuxalk Nation. Their account of the Ximkila pole states Skimina is holding Raven as he transforms into a baby, his hands reaching for the globe of light, beneath the Four Carpenters and Alhkw'ntam; the 'granddaughter of the Creator' framing is accurate. Note: the input says she 'swallows Raven and gives birth to him,' which is not in the Nuxalk Nation version, where she merely holds the transformed baby. Country should be Canada, not US.

description: South Wind is an old man in Chinook tradition who travels north along the coast. Passing the house of a giant old woman, he caught a small whale and, against her warning, cut it crossways; the cut whale turned into a huge bird. Because of this, the Chinook have always slit salmon down the back rather than across the body.
source: James Swan (1857), recorded Chinook origin story; native-languages.org archive; Franz Boas, 'Chinook Texts' (1894)
research_notes: Attested. The Old Man South Wind story (recorded as early as James Swan, 1857) explains why the Chinook slit salmon lengthwise: the giantress's warning was ignored and the whale cut crossways became a great bird. The input's 'creation of the Chinook people' is a reasonable reading of the origin narrative, though the tale primarily explains the salmon-cleaning custom.

description: The jackalope is a 'fearsome critter' of American tall-tale tradition: a jackrabbit with antelope horns, said to mimic human voices and be lured with whiskey. Popularized in Wyoming in the 1930s by taxidermist Douglas Herrick, it is a 20th-century hoax animal, not a Native American legend.

It is NOT a Native American being: the input's 'shapeshifter' framing and 'combustion' strengths are fantasy accretions; the genuine role is a tourist-industry tall-tale animal.

description: Inyan is the primordial rock of Lakota creation, the first being who existed alongside Wakan Tanka before the world began. He sacrificed his fluid power and his blood to create Maka, the Earth, and the waters, shriveling into the hard, silent stone that is the foundation of the land; in Lakota cosmology his sacrifice explains why rock and soil remain bound together.
source: Lakota creation narrative (Inyan/Maka); Wikipedia 'Lakota mythology'; native-languages.org
research_notes: Attested; expert-sourced. description: Ioskeha is the Good Twin and culture hero of Huron (Wyandot) tradition. With his evil brother Tawiscaron he shaped the world after their mother Aataentsic's death; Ioskeha created the sun and moon, slew monsters, and gave the people corn, tobacco and the arts of living. He is the model of order, light and benevolent leadership.
source: C.M. Barbeau, 'Huron and Wyandot Mythology' (1915); native-languages.org; K.L. Judson, 'Myths and Legends of the Mississippi Valley'
research_notes: Attested; expert sources (Barbeau 1915; Judson). The input's details align with the recorded accounts, though the 'sun from his mother's body' fun fact is a simplified gloss of the brothers' creation of the celestial bodies after her death.

description: Ioi is the sister of Blue Jay in Chinook tradition. Taken as a wife into the land of the dead, she tried patiently to teach her brother the customs of the ghost people, but Blue Jay mocked and mishandled everything and her warnings went unheeded. Her story is a lesson in approaching the supernatural world with humility and respect.
source: Franz Boas, 'Chinook Texts' (1894), Blue Jay and Ioi tales; native-languages.org Chinook Legends
research_notes: Attested; expert source (Boas 1894). The input's summary matches the tale, though the 'spirit-animal' archetype is a category stretch, as she is a human character in the cycle.

She is still actively worshipped today.

The legend of a man-eating 'Piasa bird' is a literary invention of John Russell (1836); the original pictograph, later destroyed and repainted, was most likely an Underwater Panther, a cougar with antlers, a scaled body and a prehensile tail.

Scholars generally identify the painted being as an Underwater Panther (Great Horned Serpent), which is never winged. The input's 'thunderbird' framing is unsupported; marked unattested as a genuine bird monster.
